**Given:** common base DC current gain \(\alpha = 0.967\); emitter current \(I_{E} = 10\) mA.
**To find:** base current \(I_{B}\).

By definition of the common base current gain,

\(\alpha = \dfrac{I_{C}}{I_{E}} \Rightarrow I_{C} = \alpha\, I_{E}\)

\(I_{C} = 0.967 \times 10 = 9.67\) mA

The three terminal currents satisfy \(I_{E} = I_{C} + I_{B}\), so

\(I_{B} = I_{E} - I_{C} = 10 - 9.67\)

\(I_{B} = 0.33\) mA

**The base current is 0.33 mA**, i.e. \(3.3 \times 10^{-4}\) A. As expected it is only about 3% of the emitter current.

**Given:** emitter current \(I_{E} = 10\) mA; collector current \(I_{C} = 9.8\) mA.
**To find:** base current \(I_{B}\).

The three terminal currents of a transistor are related by

\(I_{E} = I_{C} + I_{B}\)

\(\therefore\ I_{B} = I_{E} - I_{C} = 10 - 9.8\)

\(I_{B} = 0.2\) mA

**The base current is 0.2 mA**, i.e. \(2 \times 10^{-4}\) A — only 2% of the emitter current, as it must be for a thin, lightly doped base.

**Given:** emitter current \(I_{E} = 6.28\) mA; collector current \(I_{C} = 6.20\) mA.
**To find:** common base DC current gain \(\alpha_{DC}\).

By definition,

\(\alpha_{DC} = \dfrac{I_{C}}{I_{E}}\)

\(\alpha_{DC} = \dfrac{6.20}{6.28} = 0.98726\)

\(\alpha_{DC} \approx 0.987\)

**The common base DC current gain is 0.987.** It has no unit, being a ratio of two currents, and it is less than 1 because \(I_{C}\) is always slightly smaller than \(I_{E}\).
